6.206.m: Saubhari said: / Hearing that speech of the sage Nārada, the glorious king Śibi, Dharmarāja, / with a pleased mind, said to him, that highest one:
Śibi said: / "O sage, the glorification of this best of holy places, which awakens knowledge of the Vedas, / has been properly described by you and heard by me as destroying sin.
In this Indraprastha there are indeed hundreds of holy places, O sage. / Explain the glorification of another one also, if there is any."
Nārada said: / "O king, this Dvārakā which lies within Indraprastha— / what happened here formerly, that I tell you; listen to me:
In Kāmpilya, there was a certain twice-born man, like the flower-arrowed [Kāma] embodied; / he would captivate the hearts of all women with his foremost charms.
Skilled in the science of music, possessing the sweet voice of a cuckoo, / once, holding a lute in his hand, playing it repeatedly,
and singing with a throat sweet like the call of a cuckoo, O king of men, / that intelligent man wandered in the city from street to street.
Hearing the sound of his singing, accompanied by melodic sweeps (mūrcchanā) and tonal patterns (tāna), / the city women abandoned their household tasks and went to him.
Bewitched by his beauty, they could not endure the surge of desire; / their vital essence flowed from them upon hearing the song before them.
By whom the mind of Brahmā was enticed toward Sarasvatī, / and by whom half of Śiva's body was caused to be given to Pārvatī,
what other person in the world, even if self-controlled or possessing knowledge, / is able to conquer that Love-god (Smara)? Women are fickle by nature.
They were unable to bear the onset of love, nor could they be restrained; / what is there to say, O king? For desire is hard to conquer in the world.
Then they went there, wherever he went, / as he sang forth with voice and lute, singing enchanted by his own tones.
Then, O ruler of men, their husbands, sons, brothers, and fathers, / arriving and scolding them, led them each to their own homes.
When, searching for him, all of them went to his presence again and again, / then the citizens reported that occurrence to the ruler.
The king also, having summoned that twice-born man, asked him in private: / 'By what mantra, O vipra, have those city women been infatuated?
Tell that to me, O best of vipras, and I will give you much wealth; / otherwise, I will banish you from my kingdom, without a doubt.'
Nārada said: / Hearing this speech of the king, that best of twice-born men, / an ocean of beauty and virtue, spoke the true word before him.
The twice-born man said: / 'In me, a beggar, there is neither mantra nor herb, O king; / but all the women in your city have uncontrolled senses.
Looking at my beauty and hearing the sound of my singing, / the women in your city cannot endure the urge of love, O king.
What can I do, O great king? What fault of mine is there, O lord? / A decree [of fate] is not to be transgressed, like past karma, O protector of the earth.'
Nārada said: / While the twice-born man was speaking thus, O king Śibi of the Uśīnaras, / then all the citizens gathered together and spoke thus to the ruler of the earth.
The citizens said: / 'O king, the city women have been bewitched by this vipra; / unrestrained by us, they do not stay in the houses.

If this bewitcher of women dwells in the city, O lord, / then today itself we will surely go to other countries. / Our bull of dharma, whose essence is the rites of offering to gods and ancestors, has departed;
like the cow of sinners, this [city] has departed after him from the field; / without him, O lord of men, it has gone to ruin, abandoned by fortune.
Now they will follow him, like cows in heat following a bull. / In an empty house, how can prosperity (Lakṣmī) remain, even with effort?
Dharma, wealth, and this home—these three depend on the woman, because / the wife is dependent on dharma and wealth, and does not remain when the two are lost.'
Nārada said: / While the citizens were speaking thus, their women arrived; / seated near the king, they spoke thus to one another.
The city women said: / 'Attaining this twice-born man whose form is fair as Kāma, our minds / blossom with joy, like lotuses in water at the sight of the sun.'
[and] without him they contract, like white water-lilies without the moon. / Joining together, let us seize him as he comes before the king.
He may not be killed, and we are his; what can the ruler of the earth do?" / Nārada said: Having spoken thus, they in haste seized that best of the twice-born,
in full view of their own husbands and in front of the king as well at that time. / And they said to him: "O lord of our hearts, come to [our] homes; appease
our passion at once! Without you today we simply cannot live!" / Having heard their words, that brahmin replied:
The brahmin said: / "I am your son; you are my mothers. / Why do you abandon your homes and wander about?
Worship your own husbands, through whom both worlds are assured. / When husbands are worshipped, Viṣṇu, the lord of all the gods,
becomes pleased; and when he is pleased, what indeed is hard to obtain in this world? / The woman who, abandoning her own husband, serves another out of desire for pleasure,
incurs blame and goes to a terrifying bad rebirth. / Having dwelt there until the end of a kalpa, as long as that deceit of her husband [merits],
emerging again from that [state], she falls into the condition of an immobile being; / from that, too, she obtains the status of an animal for many births.
Released from that, in a human existence she becomes deformed in that life. / Knowing thus the destiny of sin, turn back from this person!
Otherwise, at the end of the body, you will go to a most terrible hell. / If you desire my pleasure, you will not obtain it here; / for it is sin alone for you, by which men fall down."
Nārada said: / Hearing his words and seeing the faces of their husbands, / with faces bent low in shame, they [drooped] like creepers struck down by the wind.
The most terrible fire of passion of those women of the city / subsided through the cooling water of the words of that brahmacārin.
Rising, all of them went along, reproaching Love / who brings delusion even upon the gods headed by Brahmā and Indra, O king.
The women said: / "Fie upon this evil-doing [Kāma], the axe to the timber of good conduct! / kāma [was born] for the pleasure of lovely-eyed women; blessed is he by whom Love was destroyed!
What shall we say of Rukmiṇī, adored by the world, by whose womb / was borne this one named Pradyumna, a Rāhu devouring the moon of women's virtue?
If that worst of gods should come within our range of vision, / we would cast him once more into the fire of the eye of the Lord engaged in meditation!
By Viṣṇu, who rejoices in himself, this sinner was fathered / and made the darling of sixteen thousand women—what then is our story?"
Having thus reproached Kāma, they praised that best of the twice-born, / by whom both his own conduct and theirs was preserved, O ruler of the earth.
"Blessed is the mother of that man, by whom this best of brahmins, / conqueror of Love, protector of the dharma of others, was brought forth in the world!"
"Fie on us who were conquered by desire and mocked by the king's men, / by whom grievous sin was generated through speech and mind!"
Nārada said: / Thus reflecting, those women, joined in a single mind, / all went each to her own house, enlightened by the brāhmaṇa's words.
Then the king of Kāmpilya, too, having honored that brāhmaṇa / who controlled his senses with garments and ornaments, sent him to his virtuous home.
Then, as time passed, the powerful lord of Kārūṣa / besieged the city of the lord of Kāmpilya with his armies.
A terrible battle occurred between the two; in that battle he was killed; / the entire city was looted, and the warriors were slain everywhere.
Those women, having consumed deadly poison, met their death, / but no expiation was performed by them for that sin.
By that sin, they were all born in the city / of the rākṣasa named Bhīṣaṇa as rākṣasīs of immense bodies, terrifying.
There, all those women of the city were killed by Hanumān / standing on the chariot banner of Arjuna who was protecting the sacrifice.
Again they became those very rākṣasīs in the desert wasteland, / tormented by hunger and thirst, terrifying to behold.
Thus, by that sin committed through speech and mind, / two births were obtained by them mixed with a rākṣasī womb.
By their sin, two cities along with their kings were destroyed; / therefore, one must never pursue another woman's husband.
By women fearing sin, even through speech and mind, O lord— / whether diseased, dull, poor, or deprived of both eyes— / one's own husband should not be abandoned by women desiring a good destination.

This sin generated through mind and speech by devotion to another's beloved has been related by me, / and whatever fruit was obtained by them, that also [has been related] in great detail to you, O Śibi.

From the falling of drops of water of that [Yamunā] upon their bodies, which is seen reaching Indraprastha, sinless, leading to Dvārakā, those women of the city
[…] abandoning that fierce nature of a flesh-eater born of longing for another lover in thought and speech, and attaining heaven and the state of a divine woman who brings joy to the gods.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, named ‘Description of Dvārakā’, in the Kālindīmāhātmya in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.

6.207.m: Saubhari said: / O son of Dharma, hearing these words of the great-souled / Nārada, King Śibi spoke this politely:
Śibi said: / O best of sages, from where did those rākṣasīs / dwelling on the desert road obtain water from that Dvārikā?
Nārada said: / Listen, O king, to the divine, purifying story that destroys sins, / of a brāhmaṇa named Vimala who lived in a valley of the Himavat.
In a valley of the Himavat was a brāhmaṇa named Vimala, / a worshipper of gods, sages, ancestors, and fires, a worshipper of guests,
devoted to worshipping the feet of Hari, knowing the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and dharma, / whose mind was on the Purāṇas and revelations recounting the virtues of Vāsudeva.
In his old age, by the grace of the disc-wielder, he had a son; / the father then named him Haridatta.
He performed his tonsure and other rites according to rule; / Haridatta took the Vedic metres from the presence of his guru.
Having studied the Vedas according to rule and given the guru's fee, / he renounced, detached, [forsaking] the two stages of life together with their root.
Learning of that deed, his mother, devoted to her son, wept, / bathing her pair of breasts with tears born of separation from her son.
The mother said: / Leaving me, a helpless woman, O father, where have you gone, / and your father who is seized by old age, like a bee [abandoning] reed grass?
In old age you were obtained by me through worship of the feet of the Lord of Śrī; / leaving me, you worshipped his feet for liberation!
Truly I was foolish, child, in that, having worshipped the eternal Hari, / I wished for you, who are transient, for the sake of obtaining happiness!
You are wise, my child, since you yourself worship Viṣṇu for every goal; / having known this world to be impermanent, you too have attained permanence.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Delusion cuts down my knowledge, / like an axe that violently cuts down the root of a plantain tree yielding good fruit.
Blessed is King Daśaratha, who died from grief over Rāma; / fie on me, who hold onto my life despite separation from my son!
Come, grant me a sight [of you], child, save me! / Speak words filled with the Veda before your father, O ocean of virtues!
Nārada said: / Thus lamenting, O king, his mother fell to the ground, / like the crescent of the moon [falling] from being crushed by Rāhu.
Then the brāhmaṇa sage Vimala came, O best of kings; / seeing her fallen on the ground, he said: 'What is this? What is this?'
'Why has she fallen on the ground with disheveled hair, / garments, and ornaments thrown into disarray? Is Haridatta well?'
All her female companions said to that Vimala, O king: / The companions said: / 'Having studied the Vedas and given the guru's fee,'
'Haridatta, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, has renounced the world; / in the grief of separation from him, she has fallen onto the surface of the earth.'
Nārada said: / Hearing their words, the very wise Vimala / comforted his wife with this nectar of speech:

Vimala said: / 'Arise, wife! Listen to the word spoken by me. For what reason do you grieve, fallen down? / Blessed is your son who, having realized this [world] to be perishable, worshipped the sprout-like feet of Hari!'
'You too are blessed, the giver of his birth, whose son has become a partaker of Hari's feet; / he will undoubtedly deliver me, the family, and the men born of our line, O auspicious one!'

'Where is this transient and perishable universe on the one hand, and where is the service of Hari, bestowing the eternal world, on the other? / Reflecting thus, kings such as Bharata worshipped Hari, O virtuous woman, and so indeed did your son!'
'Wife, wealth, house, body, and kinsmen—these bring sorrow in birth after birth / until a wise person, free from all desires, worships the sprout-like feet of Hari.'
Nārada said: / Thus awakened by that wise man, having risen / from the surface of the earth, she spoke to her husband in a plaintive voice.
The wife said: / 'I know all that you have spoken so well, my dear; / [yet] I do not see a bearer of the family's burden, on account of which I suffer greatly.'
'When a son is present, what need is there of a great holy place or the service of Keśava? / If our death should occur right at home, both worlds would be [secured].'
'Effort must surely be made by men to produce a good son, / because sons rescue their ancestors from the ocean of worldly existence.'
'Worship the creator and sustainer of all creatures with the desire for a son, / if you desire a son who will bear the family's burden, O highly wise one.'
Nārada said: / Hearing her words, the brāhmaṇa Vimala replied: / 'Indeed, I am going to Prayāga, the domain of Brahmā, with the desire for a son.'
Having spoken thus, the twice-born departed and went to Haridvāra; / bathing there also according to rule, he then went to Indraprastha.
After some days, O hero, in the evening, [at that place] bestowing all desires, / having bathed and eaten, he slept at night on the bank of the Yamunā.
At midnight, while he slept, Brahmā, the lord of gods, mounted upon a swan, / accompanied by all the holy sites, [came] into the presence of that pure man.
arrived and raised up Vimala, who was longing for a son; / and the best of the gods spoke words of sweet syllables.
Brahmā said: / "I know the desire that resides in your heart; / I am not able to fulfill that, so hear the reason for it.
Once on the peak of Meru all the gods assembled / and, headed by myself and Śiva, praised Mādhava for the accomplishment of their purpose.
Praised with compassion by the gods headed by us, the blessed Hari / was pleased at that time, and Viṣṇu said: 'Choose [a boon]!'
Addressed thus by him, those gods obtained from the husband of Śrī / the boon they desired, and all went to their respective abodes.
It was said by me: 'O lord of the gods, grant me an excellent boon: / May my holy place named Prayāga grant all desires!
May my second holy place situated in Indraprastha / have a hundredfold greater [merit] than that!' The whole event, O sinless one, was [told] to you by me.
Having heard those words of mine, the Blessed Lord then said to me: / “So be it,” and spoke these words again; let my words be heard.
The Blessed One said: / 'In Indra's Khāṇḍava forest is an auspicious holy place named Indraprastha, / on the bank of the Yamunā; those who die there are equal to me.
O Viriñci, my own city of Dvārakā was established there / with a hundred times more qualities than the one that stood on the shore of the ocean in ancient times.
Whatever man transgresses it and resorts to another holy place, / that man does not obtain the fruit of a holy place—what has been said is not false.
A man obtains at Śakratīrtha the religious merit spoken of all holy places; / and the city Dvārakā protects the Māyātīrtha and other holy places.
Whoever, having bathed in other holy places and performed various rites, / comes here, he will certainly obtain the fruit [of those rites] from them.'
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished; and I too, O chief of the twice-born, / went to my own world situated below Vaikuṇṭha.
Kāśī is remembered as a hundred times [more meritorious] than my holy place Prayāga; / the holy place Nigambodhaka is likewise a hundred times [more meritorious] than Kāśī.
This group of seven holy places is remembered as equal in fruit to that triad. / Whoever goes to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā without transgressing these three,
to him, O brahmin, I indeed grant what is desired, not otherwise. / Some great sages say that the merit is equal to the seven cities;
they declare Indraprastha to be a hundred times greater than those, such as Ayodhyā. / Having come here, O best of brahmins, to this holy place that yields the fruits of all desires,
indeed named Dvārakā, perform a bath out of desire for a son. / As many holy places as exist within the jar of the egg of Brahmā,
the merit is far greater than those when its hundred names are recited. / This holy place will grant you a son who will bear the burden of the family;
and through your bath Govinda will become pleased in his heart." / Nārada said: Having spoken thus, Brahmā, the god of gods, vanished there.
Vimala too bathed then and offered libations to the gods and others; / that righteous-minded one spoke thus at Dvārakā, dear to Kṛṣṇa:
"Grant me, your devotee, a son who will continue the lineage! Salutation to you!" / When spoken to thus by that brahmin, a divine voice arose at that time.
The divine voice said: / "Your son will be a knower of the truth of dharma and a perpetuator of the lineage, / through the grace of this holy place, the crest-jewel of all holy places.
Go home; do not delay; your bathing has been well performed!" / Nārada said: Hearing that voice, confident in the birth of a son,
he set out, taking water of Dvārakā in his water-pot. / On the road, a brahmin friend of his whose residence was Mount Malaya,
met [him] as he was traveling to his home after visiting holy places on all sides. / To him he recounted his own story consisting of the conversation with Brahmā,
which occurred at the Dvārakā holy place; and having heard it, he too was astonished. / And that righteous-minded one said: "O friend, hear my words!
As many holy places as are established for me in the realm of Bhārata, / that many I wish to perform at the supreme holy place spoken of by you.
Having taken me, show me, O friend, that holy place that grants all desires! / Those are excellent friends on earth who assist their friends;
neither a father, nor a mother, nor even a son is equal to them. / In this world all relatives abandon a destitute man;
but friends do not abandon him, sorrowing through his sorrow. / A friend rescues his friends immersed in the ocean of cyclic existence,
by teaching the path of devotion to Hari, which is a fire to the fuel of rebirth. / Therefore, you are my best friend; render me assistance!"
Show [me] Dvārakā, that best of sacred places, O twice-born one!"

6.208.m:
Nārada said:
Taking that twice-born one with him, Vimala arrived here at Dvārakā.
Then those two wise men bathed, desiring devotion to the Lord of Śrī.
Once again in the sky, O king, there arose a voice deep as thunder.

The voice from the sky said:
"Listen, O tigers among twice-borns! This auspicious sacred place belongs to Hari.
By the grace of this sacred place, you two will attain devotion to Viṣṇu,
by which this world abandons dreadful ignorance and delusion."

Nārada said:
Hearing that incorporeal voice, the two best of twice-borns
said to one another: "This was the grace of Hari!"

Bathing there according to the rule, having obtained supreme devotion to Hari,
they bowed down and departed, speaking thus to each other at that time.

just as the union with home, wife, and the like occurs on earth,
so now separation is inevitable, even as we journey on the road.

Likewise is it for wife, sons, and others, who stand in the mouth of Time.
Blessed is that man in the world who, understanding that association

with wife and sons is fleeting, ever takes refuge in and worships the Lord of Śrī."
Nārada said:
[Each said:] "You must remember me; I am a servant taking shelter at your feet.

A message must be sent to me." Having spoken thus, they went each to his own home.
Listen, O king, how by that friend of Vimala
liberation was effected for the demonesses as he walked along the path.
As he journeyed, that brāhmaṇa arrived at a region devoid of water,

where those demonesses, scorched by sins, were afflicted with hunger and thirst.
Then, seeing from afar that best of twice-borns walking along the path

with a water-vessel in his hand, they spoke thus to one another.
The demonesses said:
"A certain traveler is coming, holding a water-pot in his hand.

Our hunger and thirst will be somewhat appeased.
We will devour him, and we will drink the water located in the vessel

in his hand, for we have been afflicted by thirst and hunger for a hundred years!"
Nārada said:
One of them said, "First, after eating his warm liver

and then drinking his blood, I shall regain my life!"
Another said: "O elephant-faced one, how much substance is there in him?

It does not seem enough to drink even for me, who am tiger-faced!"
Another, named Rathacakrā, said: "Hear my words:

I will make an earring, and a girdle out of his entrails!"
Another said: "I, with sixteen of his teeth

blackened on one side, will play in the gambling hall, being skilled in that!"
Having spoken thus to one another, they all rushed toward that twice-born one,

with open mouths, lolling tongues, and huge arms flashing like lightning.
Seeing them approaching, the brāhmaṇa, overwhelmed with fear,

cast around himself the protection prescribed in the Vedas, O king.
Having arrived, those demonesses of terrible prowess stood at a distance,

repelled by his splendor and his mantras, O ruler of men.
And they said: "Who are you here? From where have you arrived? Tell us that!

From the sight of you our minds attain tranquility.
Will not the fruit [of liberation] arise for us from touching your feet, O vipra?
Therefore, place your own lotus-feet upon our heads!"

Nārada said:
Hearing their speech, the son of Haridatta spoke.
The twice-born said:
"Having visited holy places, I, a brāhmaṇa, have arrived.

Now I am going to Puṣkara. What is desired by you?
Ask for that, and if I am capable of giving it, I will give it then."

Deliver us by all those merits from this wretched birth,
and completely from thirst and hunger, which cause terrible suffering!"

Then I reached the holy place named Prabhāsa, situated on the seashore;
from there, I bathed at the supremely purifying Setubandha.

From there I came to most holy Kiṣkindhā,
where Vālin, the lord of the monkey troops, was slain by Rāma.

From there I came to the hermitage on the Sarasvatī situated on the bank of the Narmadā,
where Sarasvatī resides, served by all.

Then, having bowed to that confluence in the south, I entered;
there I saw the two cities, Śivakāñcī and Viṣṇukāñcī,

through death in which a creature becomes Śiva or Viṣṇu.
Then I reached Utkala, where Hari the Supreme Lord resides,

bestowing the four aims of life, the very wish of his devotees.
Having worshipped him according to rule and eaten what was offered,

which was his own prasāda, [I went to] the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having gratified the gods, sages, and ancestors there according to the rule,

I came to where the Gaṅgā becomes hundred-mouthed.
Then, having arrived at Gayā and offered funeral cakes according to the rule

to the ancestors, worshipped with tulasī, flowers, sandalwood, and water,
I came to the Sarayū in Kośala, whose waters, carried by the breeze like a helmsman,

purify all people by their touch.
There is the sacred place named Gopratāra, difficult even for the gods to attain;

there, O roamers of the night, bathing and other rites were performed by me.
Then I reached Kāśī, the capital of Umā's husband.

Bowing to Lord Viśveśvara and to Bindumādhava,
I bathed with devotion at Maṇikarṇikā and Jñānavāpī.

Dwelling there for three nights, I came again to Prayāga,
where Prajāpati himself [abides], on the fourteenth day of the bright half of Pauṣa.

Having bathed at daybreak in the single month of Māgha,
I arrived again from there at Naimiṣa on the bank of the Gomatī,

where all the sacred places dwell by their own supernatural power.
Then I reached Mathurā, where there is the sacred place named Viśrānti,

and near it the supreme holy place named Asikuṇḍa,
and the sacred places Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, Dhruvatīrtha, Akrūratīrtha, Keśitīrtha, and Kālīyatīrtha.

There is the Yamunā, highly auspicious, granting all desired objects.
On both of her banks are twelve forests, shining with beauty,

O roamers of the sky, fulfilling all purposes.
Having bathed and drunk in them, a man is not born again.

Then I came to holy and supreme Hastināpura,
where the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, born from the lotus-foot of the Lord of Śrī, [flows].

Then, having arrived at the abode of Nārāyaṇa situated in the land of the Himavat
and having seen Mādhava, I came to Kedāra.

Having worshipped the Lord of the Universe there and drunk the water of the Haṃsodaka,
I came again to highly sacred Haridvāra on the bank of the Jāhnavī.

Bathing there and gratifying the ancestors, gods, and sages,
I came to Kurukṣetra, where the eastward-flowing Sarasvatī lies.

There too, with my senses restrained, I performed all rites.
And having worshipped the lotus-foot of the Lord of Śrī, toward Puṣkara

I departed. On the way, however, my friend named Vimala,
going home from the holy place Indraprastha, met me.
I was taken back by that twice-born man, O demonesses, / to that holy ford, Śakraprastha, which grants all aims,
where holy Dvārakā is situated, fashioned by Viṣṇu himself. / There Viṣṇu was directly perceived by his voice, not by form.
There he and I bathed together to attain devotion to Viṣṇu; / that devotion was granted to me and to him by Viṣṇu appearing in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard the voice of Hari there, though no form was seen, / devotion was obtained from that place; hence I am going toward Puṣkara.
This holy water held in my water-pot belongs to that lord of holy places / called Dvārakā, O night-roaming women, I tell you.
Since you asked me, this is what I have related to you. / Seeing this wretched condition of yours, compassion arises in my heart.
Speak: what shall I do today? For I am at your disposal. / May knowledge come to you! Saying this, he sprinkled them with the water.
Touched by that water, having remembered all their actions / from past births, they discarded their dreadful demon body.
Having attained a divine body and mounted the seven celestial chariots that arrived, / becoming apsarases, they bowed to the twice-born man.
And they said: 'O best of the twice-born, through contact with the water of Dvārakā, / we have been released from the state of demons and are going to the abode of the gods.
O twice-born, this Dvārakā situated within Indraprastha— / there is no other holy place in the world superior to it that grants all aims.'
Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, O king, mounted on celestial chariots, / they went toward the eastern quarter, permitted by that twice-born man.
Hearing this glorification of Dvārakā situated on the bank of the Yamunā, / a man is freed from sins, O king.
Whatever fruit arises from feeding a hundred brāhmaṇas versed in the Veda / according to their desires, that arises from hearing this glorification.
Just as there is sensual happiness in proper worship of Govinda, / so it is from hearing the glorification of this Dvārakā, O king.
Whatever fruit is attained from giving twenty palas of gold during an eclipse of the sun or moon, / that is obtained by one hearing her glorification.
Hearing of the obtaining of a son by Vimala, a son is attained in this world; / hearing of the attainment of devotion by his friend, supreme devotion is attained.
Whoever full of faith hears of the liberation of the demonesses, / he goes, just like them, to the supreme abode of the gods in a celestial chariot.

O best of kings, the glory of Dvārakā, served by the people of the three worlds / and situated at Śakratīrtha, has been described to you; / what other exceedingly holy matter should I relate before you? / Speak, for no delay should be made regarding one's own welfare.

6.209.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / O Saubhari, the glorification of which holy place situated at Śakratīrtha / did the sage Nārada describe to Śibi?
A desire to hear arises in me regarding this, O best of sages; / recount to me, who am bowed, the holy dialogue between Śibi and Nārada.
Saubhari said: / O Dharmarāja, King Śibi, having heard the glorification of Dvārakā / described by Nārada, asked him with reverence.
Śibi said: / O son of Brahmā, best of gods, the excellent and wondrous glorification / of Dvārakā situated on the bank of Indraprastha has been heard by me.
If there is any purifying account regarding Ayodhyā, O sage, / recount that to me, who am thirsty for the nectar of your speech.
Nārada said: / In this regard there is a holy story that destroys great sins, / concerning an anciently engaged barber and a twice-born man named Mukunda.
The barber was a slayer of a brāhmaṇa, O king, and the twice-born man met an untimely death; / yet through the grace of Kośalā, both went to the heavenly realm.
That city was settled on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river; / there lived a sinful and despicable barber named Caṇḍaka.
A committer of sin, he was a stealer of others' wealth by theft; / a murderer with weapons, nooses, and the like, and a plunderer of wayfarers.
Always addicted to gambling and liquor, his senses lecherous after other men's wives, / breaking down the wall of a temple, he was a seller of bricks and stones.
Near his residence lived a brāhmaṇa endowed with fortune, / knower of Vedic rituals, named Mukunda, O king.
Once, having embraced his young wife, / he fell asleep fearlessly at night, his limbs slack from the exhaustion of lovemaking.
Then, in the dead of night, Caṇḍaka entered that dwelling / of Mukunda in order to steal whatever items such as ornaments were in the mansion.
Taking whatever was outside the royal tent, he went to his house, / and then entered that brāhmaṇa's house again.
Desiring to rip open the door, he made a great effort, / but, blocked by an iron mechanism, he was unable to open it.
Then he climbed up and entered the house of that brāhmaṇa; / having entered that house, cruel, holding a dagger in his hand,
that most wicked barber, engaged in thievery, reached the upper story; / there he saw the married couple deeply asleep, overcome with lovemaking.
And he went to their side with a desire to take the golden ornaments; / having taken many ornaments lying on one side of the bed,
that barber stretched out his hand to seize [the rest] from his body. / At the thief's touch, the brāhmaṇa awoke, stricken with fear.
He said nothing; closing his eyes, he remained right there. / When that sinful thief, having taken the ornaments from the body,
moved away, he was seized with both arms by that twice-born man, / who, coming from behind, could not bear the loss of his wealth.
Then by that thief, O king, the twice-born man was struck with a dagger; / with the middle of his belly torn open, he cried out: 'Father! Mother!'
Saying 'What is this? What is this?', people came to his side; / they saw him with his intestines fallen out and his body smeared with blood.
And they asked: 'Mukunda, by whom has such a deed been done?' / He too, with great difficulty, spoke this to his kinsmen:
Mukunda said: / 'This is the ripening of deeds previously accumulated by myself alone; / no one is the giver of happiness or sorrow to any embodied being.
Righteousness and unrighteousness performed in the past are the sole roots of them.' / Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, deeply tormented by immense pain,
he abandoned his life-breaths, O king, while his friends were looking on. / Then, O king, his mother, a virtuous twice-born woman, lamented,
placing on her lap his head adorned with earrings. / The mother said: / 'Alas, I am ruined by you reaching your final state, my child,
as the beauty of day [is lost] by the sun sinking down the western mountain! / That body of yours, O wise one, which was worthy of being anointed with sandalwood paste,
is now covered with dust, plunging me into an ocean of anguish and grief!

That practice of chewing betel which was observed by you, / is certainly being imitated now mixed with an outpouring of blood! / Those eyes of yours that previously conquered the splendor of the lotus,
have now become as if enveloped by a mass of darkness! / Arise, arise, child! Teach your pupils!
Properly honor the guest who has arrived at the end of the Vaiśvadeva rite! / Your companions standing at the door are calling you; go to them!'

"Give to them what is to be given, and take what is to be taken.
Alas, alas! Give me an answer; I fall at your feet!

Otherwise, I shall give up my life right by your side!"
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the mother of that Mukunda then fainted.

His wife, placing his head upon her lap, lamented.
The wife said:
"O ocean [of virtues]! Hear my words through the channel of [your] ears!

If you are angry with your mother, tell me why, before me.
Never before, O virtuous one, did you keep such silence!
Has an insult been done to you by any younger brother?

This parrot in the cage does not eat food without you;
feed him the well-cooked grain, and the sweet-voiced starling [too]!

'Rāma, Rāma, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu'—arise
and make both of these clever birds, the starling and the parrot, recite the series of names!

What offence have I committed against you, that you do not speak to me?
Whatever wealth you gave to me, I have well preserved it.

O lord, what splendor of your own was placed by you in my womb—
not awaiting the time of its birth, I shall follow after you!"

Nārada said:
Having thus lamented, that beloved wife of Mukunda then
did not weep, [being] a virtuous woman resolved to follow her husband [in death].

Then the guru of that Mukunda, named Vedāyana,
a wandering renunciant, arrived at his house, O king.

"Where has Mukunda gone? And the wise one's mother and wife
are not seen?"—thus questioned by him then, a servant-girl reported:

Having died, he lies fallen on the floor upon the upper terrace of the mansion;
his mother, his wife, and his brothers are beside him.

Fallen into a great ocean of grief, they are lamenting, O guru!"
Nārada said:
Having heard that speech uttered by the servant-girl, the wandering ascetic,

ascending the mansion, saw his disciple dead,
and seeing his relatives near him weeping bitterly,

wishing to rescue them from the ocean of grief, that steadfast man said:
Vedāyana said:
"Is this grief of yours felt with reference to the body, or to the soul?

O mother, tell me the truth; indeed, it is not fitting for either.
This body is an aggregate of material elements, acquired through past deeds.

When those [deeds] are exhausted, separation of the elements occurs.
That unification of them through actions is [what is called] birth for humans;

upon their destruction, there is their separation, and that is considered death.
Because the union and separation of the elements is dependent upon action, according to the wise,

therefore, no grief should be felt for the body, which is helpless and insentient.
Birth and death are perceived in the soul through beginningless ignorance.

Through the notion of 'I' regarding the body, one thinks [so] in the self, and not without it;
upon its cessation, that [reality] is Brahman, which is pure and devoid of form,

self-luminous, the cause of the world, beyond causes, free from the qualities,
eternal, consciousness and bliss, illuminating the world by its own radiance.

The tongue does not taste it, the eye does not see [it], nor does the ear hear [it];
the nose does not smell [it], and the skin never touches [it].

Beyond the sense organs, it is self-luminous and beholds the self;
free from sensory objects, distant from the mind, not even an object of the intellect.

Its incarnation-forms are pure sattva; the gods
worship [them], but they do not know the form that is beyond the real and the unreal.

For the soul whose nature is such, what fool would harbor
grief with regard to it, since it has neither origination nor destruction?"
Thus [ends …] in the Kālindīmāhātmya in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.

6.210.m:
Nārada said:
Having thus enlightened them all with words on ultimate reality,
that ascetic caused the rites originating from the self to be performed for him.

The pregnant wife of Mukunda, who made an insistent effort
to follow her husband, was prevented by that wise man.

Taking his bones together with that renunciant,
his brother set out to cast them into the waters of the Gaṅgā, O king.

Those two, the Brahmin and the renunciant, after some days, O king,
arrived in company with a caravan of people here at the sacred site Indraprastha.

Within Indraprastha lies this Kośalā, O king;
here on the bank of the Yamunā the two slept at night upon the ground,

having placed the cloth packet containing the bones between the two of them.
Exhausted from the weariness of the road, the two entered the state of deep sleep.

Then, at midnight, while the caravan travelers were fast asleep,
a solitary dog arrived there, wishing to carry off cooked food and the like.

He wandered through the entire camp, repeatedly smelling places such as the cooking areas,
licking vessels, now and then enduring blows of a stick on his head.

Struck on the head by someone, he fled silently from there,
unable to retaliate, just like a henpecked man before his own wife.

Where that dog was beaten with sticks, stones, bricks, and the like,
he entered again right there, desiring to obtain vessels with food,

just as an affectionate but impoverished man [frequents] courtesans out of desire for pleasure.
Wandering thus, he came also right to where both of them were sleeping.

The dog seized the cloth packet from between them;
having carried that cloth packet a little distance,

and tearing it with his teeth, seeing the bones inside devoid of flesh,
he cast them into the midst of the waters of this Kośalā.

As soon as those bones were thrown into this water by him, O lord of the earth,
Mukunda, mounted upon a celestial aerial chariot, arrived there.

Seeing his guru and his younger brother asleep, he gently awakened them then,
and having saluted the guru, the celestial-formed one spoke, O king.

Mukunda said:
"O guru Vedāyana, salutations to you! Blessings to you, younger brother!
Indeed, through your favor my bones have fallen into this sacred bathing place.

Having met this death and attained hell as its fruit,
by the grace of this sacred bathing place, a divine destination has been obtained by me.

I have come here to pay homage to you, the guru who has become a sacred shrine,
while I am going to the abode of the thirty [gods] in a celestial chariot.

You have been saluted, as well as this sacred bathing place and this brother;
I have been seen, now grant me leave: I go to heaven, the arising of joy!"

Nārada said:
Having heard this speech of Mukunda, his guru then,
Vedāyana, free from astonishment, spoke to him seated in the aerial chariot.

Devāyana said:
"O Mukunda, tell me the truth: having met death,
to which world did you go, dear child, from which you are now going to heaven?

What happened to you there, my dear? Who is the ruler of that world?
What kind of subjects are there, and what kind of justice? Tell everything!"

When I was struck down by that evil-minded barber Caṇḍaka,
then the exceedingly terrifying servants of Yama arrived,

tawny-eyed, with red hair, dark bodies, nails, and lips,
dwarf-like, with long feet, short noses, and projecting teeth.

'Let him be taken, let him be taken by the order of Dharmarāja
to the city of Saṃyamanī!'—thus they spoke to one another.
Having spoken thus, placing me in a body of torment with immense wrath, / binding me with cruel bonds, they beat me with iron clubs.
As I was being led by them along a road of scorching sand, / I wept, afflicted with great sorrow, and was struck again by them.
They made [their hold] secure and spoke, reproaching me greatly. / The messengers of Yama said: / 'Since you neglected your guru while firmly professing the Veda,
what will you do before Yama? His terrible face must be faced! / You must suffer the terrible fruit of that sin.
Because of that very sin, O sinner, you met an untimely death.' / Having spoken thus, within an hour they brought me to [the city] situated many leagues away,
the city Saṃyamanī, where King Yama himself resides. / Bowing to Dharmarāja and placing me before him,
they reported me, saying: 'This sinful twice-born has been brought.' / Then Dharmarāja, having looked at me, spoke to the members of his assembly.
Yama said: / 'O assembly members, listen to my words with attentive minds: / When I was appointed to this office by Brahmā,
then he, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said to me: / Brahmā said: / 'You are the chastiser of unrighteous men, the lord of Saṃyamanī.

Inflict punishment according to the transgression, O son of the Sun! / He who, though capable, does not support his parents, and he who injures his guru— / these two are great sinners and must be cast into the hells by you,
into all [hells], until each [term] amounts to ten thousand years. / You must never show mercy to these two, O lord of the quarters!'
Yama said: / 'Thus, by the command of Brahmā, O members of the assembly, / I show no [favor] to a man who harms his guru, nor to one who fails to support his parents.
This brāhmaṇa injured his guru; through that injury he attained an untimely death. / Brought by my servants at my command, he is unfit even to be seen.
O servants, cast him first into the terrible Raurava for ten thousand years, / and then, having removed him from there, cast him into another!
Indeed, for that very same amount of time this sinner who neglected his guru / must remain in all the hells successively according to their allotted periods!'
Mukunda said: / 'O master Vedāyana, O guru, by Yama's order your servants / took me, bound me with cords, and threw me into the terrible Raurava.
There I suffered immense and most dreadful torment; / then even a single moment spent there seemed like an age, O father!
For thirty days that misery was endured by me while staying there; / but on this thirty-first day I came forth.
When the pieces of my bones fell into this most supreme sacred place, / the sin born of neglecting my guru was instantly destroyed.
And by the favor of this sacred place, I have attained the heavenly realm; / I shall dwell happily in heaven as long as there are fourteen Indras.
The beings who dwell in that city of Yama / bring terror to sinners, but to the righteous they are charming.
With faces like lions, elephants, or boars, having huge fangs and protruding bellies, / cat-faced, red-haired, wrathful women with long feet and hands—
when I became free from sin by the grace of this sacred place, / then I saw the beings in Yama’s abode endowed with divine form:
all of them speaking truth, full of modesty and good conduct, / wearing divine ornaments, adorned with celestial garments.
All this has been told, O dear one, what was asked by you, O sinless one. / Permit me now to go toward the city of the lord of the immortals.
Nārada said: / Having heard these words spoken by his disciple, / the righteous ascetic questioned that twice-born Mukunda once more, O king.
Vedāyana said: / 'From childhood, with a guru's affection, all was studied by you from me— / the Veda accompanied by grammar, along with the word-by-word and step-by-step recitation.
Excellent service was rendered to me by you with devotion. / In you are found the qualities of the virtuous, O good one, such as tranquility and self-restraint.
How did the sin caused by neglecting a guru arise in you? / Relate this to me, O dear one, so that I may know it in truth.'

Mukunda said: / 'The givers of birth, the sacred thread, and a bride, as well as the teacher of the Veda— / never was a violation of the command of the giver of the sacrificial thread committed by me.
Service to my mother-in-law and father-in-law was performed by me just like a servant; / nor was any violation of your command committed by me, who imparted the scriptures to me.
There was a family priest and spiritual guide, completely versed in the Veda and Vedānta; / an offense was committed against him by me; please hear regarding that, O venerable one.
Whenever a son is born in our family, O you who know dharma, / then to that priest a cow or dakṣiṇā for it is given,
and the umbilical cord is cut by him: such is the custom of our lineage. / Formerly, when my own son was born on an auspicious day,
the family rite was not performed by me, whose mind was foolish; / and solely by not performing it did I become one who neglected his guru.
All this has been reported, how sin accrued to me through neglecting a guru. / Grant me permission: I am going to the abode of the gods.'
Vedāyana said: / 'Situated within Indraprastha is this auspicious Kośalā; / by its grace, memory of a former birth is seen.
By what merit did your bones fall into this sacred place, / O Mukunda? Relate this, if memory of it remains with you, O sinless one.'
Mukunda said: / 'A certain brāhmaṇa came to my house in the evening; / lodging and food were given to him by me according to rule.
He too, having eaten to his content, fell asleep on an auspicious couch. / In the middle of the night, a very severe fever came upon his entire body.
His whole body tormented by it, the twice-born gained no sleep; / and just at dawn he gave up his life-breaths, death having arrived.
His cremation and other funeral rites were performed by me, O guru, / and his bones were cast into the Gaṅgā in accordance with the injunctions.
By that merit, my bones fell in this auspicious / sacred place named Kośala, fashioned by Brahmadeva.'

Nārada said: / Having thus recounted his own history, O king, that twice-born, instantly possessing a body beautiful as a deity's, went to heaven by aerial carriage. / This I have told you: having met death at the hands of a thief, he obtained heaven by the grace of this king among sacred places.

6.211.m: Nārada said: / The whole excellent narrative of Mukunda has been related before you, O Śiva; / now hear from me that of the barber Caṇḍaka as well.
On the day the brāhmaṇa Mukunda was killed by him, / by Caṇḍaka, then, O king, that news was heard by the citizens.
Having heard it, they reported it clearly before the king. / The citizens said: / 'Mukunda, the best of brāhmaṇas, has been killed by Caṇḍaka, O king,
and his abundant wealth has been carried off. Let what is appropriate be done! / For you are the protector of us subjects, and the punisher of the wicked.'
Nārada said: / Having heard this, the king, his eyes red with anger, / spoke to the minister standing at his side: 'Listen to what these people are saying!
Bring that sinner quickly, or else I will have you killed! / Rise, rise, [seize] the greatest sinner, and let peace be brought to the virtuous!'
"In whose realm the subjects are oppressed by fierce robbers, / that king goes to hell if he does not protect them from those [robbers]."
Nārada said: / Hearing this word of the king, the minister, along with Śiva, O king, / swiftly mounted a horse accompanied by a hundred foot-soldiers.
He went to the house of Mukunda and asked his relatives: / "By whom was Mukunda slain? Speak the truth before me!
I will kill that wicked man by command of the king!" / Nārada said: / Hearing this speech of the minister, the brāhmaṇa's relatives replied:
The brāhmaṇa's relatives said: / "O minister, Mukunda was slain by Caṇḍaka the barber! / Indeed, this turban fell from him as he fled.
That evil-doer was seen with her own eyes by the wife of Mukunda himself. / What shall we do? By that wicked man we have been plunged into an ocean of grief!"
Nārada said: / Hearing this word of the relatives of the brāhmaṇa, / that minister went to the house of that wicked barber.
Dismounting quickly from his horse, he entered that house himself / together with several foot-soldiers and saw him sleeping.
Then, ordered [by him], the foot-soldiers dragged by the hair that instant / and raised from the bed that wicked, vile barber.
Muttering, "What? What?", as he opened his eyes, / just as that wicked barber [awoke], so he saw him before [him].
Remembering his own deed, the sin that he had committed in the night, / he stood for a moment with downcast face, seeing Yama poised over his head.
Having caused that wicked man to be seized by his foot-soldiers, the minister / brought him to the king's presence and spoke thus to the ruler of the earth:
"O king, this Caṇḍaka the barber, a slayer of a brāhmaṇa, has been brought. / Whatever you command, my master, I shall do swiftly."
The king said: / "O best of ministers, knower of dharma, listen to my words: / This excellent river, the Candrabhāgā, is pure, O long-lived one.
Those who abandon their life-breaths here attain the realm of the gods. / Therefore, this wicked-souled barber must not be killed here.
Beyond five krośas, outside its border, / let this slayer of a brāhmaṇa go without delay to the terrible hells!"
Nārada said: / Being told thus by that king, that best of ministers, O king, / sent out outcasts to slay him by the command of the monarch.
Those outcasts took him up, and on the other bank of the Candrabhāgā, / at a distance of two yojanas, they severed his head.
That wicked man became a serpent in the Mārwār desert, an embodiment of death, / dwelling inside the hollow of a dhava tree, with a face dreadful from flames of poison.
That dhava tree became dried up by the fire of his hiss, / just as a full lake [dries up] by the heat of the sun.
From the passage of that wicked man, the root of every tree was blasted; / grass and other vegetation were destroyed, becoming harmful to animals.
Once, a caravan arrived there from the southern country, / travelling to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa named Badarī, O auspicious king.
There a certain brāhmaṇa joined the caravan on the road; / carrying on his shoulder a seamless wooden casket / containing the bones of his father and mother,
he was going in order to cast them, O king, / into the water of the Gaṅgā, O highly fortunate one, which grants wishes even to sinners.
He too arrived at that forest where that serpent resided. / Setting down the casket in a secluded spot, [which had] a bolt made of iron,
then coming there, that serpent struck the bolt with his hood; / when it opened slightly, he entered into the casket.
The bolt returned to its place, and then that coiled serpent, / terrible with poison, remained motionless right there in the casket.
Then at dawn, all of them departed from that place, O king. / That brāhmaṇa too, having placed the casket covered with a blanket
upon his head, O king of kings, moved toward the river of Jahnu. / In a few days, that caravan of pilgrims reached
this very purified [place] Kośalā, O lord of the earth. / Then, distressed by the cold, the vipra uncovered the blanket,

the covering of the casket, O king, there on the auspicious bank at Ayodhyā. / That serpent, starved of food, having obtained wind as food,

He went outside from it, having cast away the slender peg; / seeing him come out, [he said] in anger: “A snake, a snake!”
all the people came forward shouting, with clods of earth in hand. / While the serpent was fleeing, he was struck down by one of them.
He then gave up his life-breaths before the eyes of the pilgrims. / Abandoning the serpent's body, he attained godhood, so hard to obtain.
Mounting a celestial chariot, he spoke this to the people there: / The serpent said: / "O southern brāhmaṇas, listen to my words!
Formerly, I was a vile barber named Caṇḍaka, a slayer of a brāhmaṇa. / Due to the grave sin of brahmahatyā, I became a serpent in the desert wasteland.
After experiencing the torments of hell for five hundred thousand years, / twenty thousand years have passed in my serpent womb.

By the grace of this tīrtha, exalted godhood has been attained. / Therefore, this tīrtha named Kośalā must never be abandoned; / it grants all aims, since heaven has been attained even by a sinner such as I!"
Nārada said: / Thus that wicked barber, having reached a reproached womb, / mounted a celestial chariot and went to heaven by the grace of this tīrtha.
Those southerners, having become ascetics right there in that tīrtha / whose glory was witnessed, dwelt with their minds fixed on Govinda's lotus-feet.
Having seen the glory of this tīrtha, that best of brāhmaṇas, / inspired with faith in this tīrtha, cast the bones of his parents [into it].
When the pieces of bone fell, his two parents that very moment / arrived there divine, mounted on an excellent celestial chariot.
And they said to their own son while the people were listening: / "Child, live long in the world, blessed with wealth and grain!

And by bestowing liberation upon us, you too shall attain liberation—this is not false! / Whatever fruit there is for a son by giving the piṇḍa in the Gaṅgā, / and whatever destination there is for the ancestors, both happen here from the immersion of the bones."

6.212.m: Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, the two parents of that vipra, endowed with divine forms, / mounted an excellent celestial chariot and went to the city of Hari.
Their son, having stayed right there in Kośalā for three days, / went to his own home, contemplating the glory of the tīrtha.
Kośalā is praised in this very manner by the wise, O king. / I shall narrate that to you whose mind is eager to hear.
Those southern religious students, desiring to die, dwelt in it, / in Kośalā which grants all desires to those facing death.
Then a certain one among them, disregarding that Kośalā, / was going to the place of Nārāyaṇa, but was stopped on the way by Viṣṇu
in the form of an old brāhmaṇa, who spoke thus to that dvija: / The old brāhmaṇa said: / "Where are you going, O best of brāhmaṇas, having abandoned this auspicious Kośalā?
This Indraprastha tīrtha is the best of all tīrthas, O dvija; / for here, my son, this Kośalā bestows liberation and is beloved by Viṣṇu."
Wherever you go leaving this [place] which grants the desireless state, / no attainment will occur there, and Viṣṇu will turn his face away from you.
If you desire liberation, O twice-born, take up residence in this holy ford. / For according to whatever desire you bathe, it will grant that very aim.
Before your very eyes, O twice-born, even a serpent would attain godhood. / By its grace, the twice-born couple attained heaven in liberation.
Even though you have gained faith from seeing its greatness, / having attained it by the rise of fortune, how can you abandon it?
Just as someone afflicted with thirst, even after reaching an ocean of nectar, / leaves it and goes toward muddy water, so you appear foolish.
Just as someone, bewitched, throws a wish-fulfilling jewel that was in his hand / into a well—the same condition seen in him is seen in you.
Just as some foolish man, having worshipped Viṣṇu the lord of the universe, / asks for trivial sensual pleasure—the same condition is yours.
One should not depart, leaving this Kośalā that bestows all aims of life. / For one who bathes here, heaven is attained; for one who dies [here], an immortal dwelling [is attained].

Nārada said:
O king, having heard the words of Hari who had assumed the form of an elderly twice-born, / that twice-born spoke to the twice-born, praising Badarikāśrama:

The twice-born said:
O best of twice-born, faith does not arise from your speech, / for I have previously heard of the glory of this small village.
I have never heard of this sacred ford called Indraprastha. / Whence, then, O old man, is this Kośalā situated within it?
Where Nārāyaṇa is directly present and where yogins are liberated— / leaving that holy hermitage, how can I remain here, O twice-born?
If Viṣṇu himself were to come and restrain me, saying thus: / 'O twice-born, this Indraprastha is a sacred site superior to Badarī,'
then, having set out from my home desiring liberation, I would not proceed / to that hermitage; otherwise my stay here cannot be.

Nārada said:
When spoken to thus by that twice-born, four-armed Hari / cast off his ordinary form and manifested, wearing a divine form.
just as the Himālaya is among mountains, just as the king of birds is among birds; / just as Indra is among the thirty gods, just as Nārada is among Vaiṣṇavas;
just as the sun is among luminous bodies, and just as the ocean of milk is among oceans; / just as a brāhmaṇa is among castes, and the Grandfather among creations;
just as the son born of Kauśalyā is supreme among the incarnations of Viṣṇu— / so is this Śakraprastha supreme among all sacred fords.
Whether without desire or filled with desire, when a man goes to any sacred ford, / I alone, the soul of all, am the dispenser of fruits in each and every place.
Whoever leaves Kośalā, which is situated within Indraprastha, and departs, / he, though a devotee, does not obtain the fruit from me, the giver of boons and protector of the multitudes.

Nārada said:
Having thus heard his words and having seen that supreme form, / having bowed down to the beloved of Ramā, the twice-born went to that very [Kośalā].
The Lord too, the all-pervading soul of the universe, vanished at once, / having pointed out the truth to that twice-born and worshipped with that disposition by him.
Having arrived there in Kośalā, O ruler of men, that twice-born / related that entire event to all his companions.
Those twice-born from the south, having also heard it from the fortunate one, / engaged in fasting there and cast off their ordinary bodies.
Just then, mounted upon Garuḍa, the venerable Viṣṇu approached / accompanied by celestial vehicles and by his retinues, brilliant with light.
Seeing him arriving with his celestial vehicle and his host, / they fell flat like a stick on the earth with divine forms.
And all the twice-born, possessing bodies endowed with divine knowledge, / praised that god of divine form whose lotus feet are worshipped by gods.

The brāhmaṇas said:
Salutations to you who possess a body with the luster of the atasi flower and are wrapped in yellow garments, / having various gems set in shining earrings, a dark cloud spanning the sky with lightning at his ears!
Devotion to you is truly a wish-fulfilling creeper: when resorted to, it grants the heart's desire; / just so is your Kośalā, O Lord—by your grace both are attained by people.
We bow to your lotus feet, revered by the gods headed by Īśvara, / meditated upon in the heart by assemblies of yogins, the source of supreme bliss, the realm of liberation.

We have fully attained, O Lord of Śrī, your true form marked by graceful signs such as the Śrīvatsa; / nevertheless, we desire servitude to you, which has been attained and honored by all headed by Nārada.

That happiness of those who have attained servitude to you is not even known by Lakṣmī dwelling within your chest; / O Lord of Śrī, glorious Maheśa knows it; no other person in the world has experienced it.

Among us, your servants, O Lord of Śrī, he is honorable even to those free from passion; / therefore the foremost sages headed by Nārada worship the Lord of the world through those who have attained your devotion.

Even Śambhu, whose inner self has experienced the bliss of Brahman, attains satisfaction in serving you; / to grasp your virtues again and again, devoted to you and filled with emotion, he dances wildly.

For this reason, when embodied beings attain your servitude, the waves [of saṃsāra] do not arise; / those two doorkeepers marked with your emblems, having reached their own abode through delusion, [...]
Without your will, a sudden fall from that world is never initiated for the people of your realm. / Who here could know your Māyā, difficult to comprehend even by gods headed by Brahmā and Śarva?

Nārada said:
Thus being praised by them, the Lord, ready to go to his own abode, / spoke to those southerners in a voice deep as a thundercloud.

The Blessed Lord said:
O twice-born, by the grace of this Kośalā you have attained / assimilation into my form, and you shall also attain servitude to me.
From this day forth, O twice-born, this supreme sacred ford / shall be loudly renowned by the name of Southern Kośalā.
Where, having become the son of Daśaratha, I shall slay the ten-headed [Rāvaṇa]— / that is proclaimed by all the best of sages as Northern Kośalā.
He who dies endowed with knowledge in that [Northern Kośalā] ascends to Vaikuṇṭha; / even he who dwells in it without that goes to heaven.
Therefore they proclaim this Southern Kośalā to be ten times greater; / some foremost sages rightly declare it to be eleven times greater.
Such is the distinction between that one and this one, in my view: / those who die in that one, these retinues of mine lead to Vaikuṇṭha;
him who dies in this one with his mind fixed on none other, I myself, / placing him upon Garuḍa and bestowing assimilation into my form, convey to that [abode].

Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and having taken those twice-born, Viṣṇu went to Vaikuṇṭha, / himself praising the greatness of this sacred ford, O king.
This whole reason has been recounted to you, O ruler of the earth, / on account of which this is called Southern Kośalā here by the wise.

The greatness of Kośalā, which destroys the multitude of impurities of the Kali age for men who hear it and is desired for attaining the feet of the lotus-eyed Lord, has been described to you, O best of kings; / as you listen, I shall tell you the account that took place in Madhuvana.

6.213.m: Nārada said: / This Madhuvana, dear one, is auspicious and supremely purifying. / Pleased with the king of gods, Viṣṇu established this city.
Here is the sacred bath named Viśrānti, the best in the three worlds, / bestowing liberation upon men who know, purifying, frequented by the virtuous.
Always the Soul of the Universe, Viṣṇu, bearing the form of the holy Boar, / dwells here, O king, at this supreme holy place named Viśrānti.
By him who has constantly worshipped Viṣṇu through many births, / death is indeed attained at this holy place, O king.
A second one was made by Hari right on the bank of the Kālindī, / named the Viśrānti sacred bath, where Kaṃsa was struck down.
These two are equal, O king, in their qualities that bestow Vaikuṇṭha; / by some rise of fortune is [this place], which gives all ends of life, attained.
Now I will relate the glorification of this holy place before you, / by hearing which you will obtain the fruit of bathing in all sacred waters.
In the valley of the Himālaya, in the auspicious city of Kirātas, / there lived a brāhmaṇa named Kuśala, O king, who was impoverished.
His wife was of evil conduct, devoted to a man of vile behavior; / by her actions, that wretched adulteress thoroughly deluded her husband.
Deluded by her, the husband was unable to restrain her; / intent on her commands, miserable, he became just like someone bought with money.
People mocked that twice-born man, the husband of an unchaste wife; / out of fear of mockery, that foolish man did not even leave the house.
She wore costly silks and ornaments / given by her paramours; wicked-minded, even when laughed at she felt no shame.
Old clothing cast off from the body of a slave girl / the wicked woman gave with contempt to her own husband.
Thus insulted by that unchaste woman, her own husband, / having fallen into extreme grief, took poison and died at night.
Terrified of the king because of that sin, the wanton woman then / uttered a false word: 'I shall follow my husband.'
Her female friends, having been instructed by her in this way, approached her / and restrained her, speaking to her as follows, O lord of the earth.
The friends said: / 'O fawn-eyed woman, why are you doing such a ruinous thing, / by which you are prepared to destroy your body that resembles gold?
What pleasure did you see from that inactive man, / poor, incapable, O friend, filling only his own belly?
Protect this young son; except for you, who is his protector? / If you die, O beautiful one, all of us shall die.
Look upon this house, arise, O fair-faced one! / May this son of yours live long, who will bring happiness in the three worlds.
All your kinsmen desire your life; / arise and fulfill the wish of your own relatives.
All your female companions weep out of affection for you, O virtuous lady; / by giving your word, hold back these deeply sorrowful women.'
Nārada said: / Having heard their words, famous for duty, the wicked woman / raised her face and said, making her own kinsmen hear:
The friend said: / 'The word of righteousness spoken by you, I know it is true indeed; / yet one's own husband must be honored by women, for he gives both worlds.
The statement which is spoken by me is endowed with the treatises on righteousness; / listen to that word, O friends, and if it is fitting, give your assent.
The woman who faithfully follows her deceased husband, / even if sinful, dwells for a long time in heaven with him alone.
A husband must not be abandoned by women, even if penniless or diseased; / living or dead he is to be followed: this is the eternal sacred tradition.
Reflecting thus in my heart, O friends, I shall follow my own husband; / he [my son] will fare by his own destiny; what indeed can I do for him?'
Nārada said: / Addressed thus by her, those friends, wicked and giving wicked counsel, / spoke to her with words of righteousness, beguiling all the people.
The friends said: / 'Kill us first, O fair-browed one, and afterwards follow your beloved! / We are all unable to bear separation from you.
For you who kill us and follow your own husband, / the merit will be small, the sin abundant; and what kind of attainment of heaven will there be?
While alive, your own husband was well maintained; / what was prescribed for husband and wife, all that was done by you, O friend.
As long as he is unable to provide the means for his own life, / so long will your son live by your good fortune.'
Nārada said: / Thus addressed, she turned back from following her husband; / she then caused the funeral rites to be performed by her son.
Then after some time, she turned her mind to the sacred-thread ceremony of her son, / and had it performed by brāhmaṇas, giving money bestowed by her paramours.
His thread-investiture performed, that boy, born of adultery, possessed the knowledge of true reality; / leaving home immediately, he became devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Attaining the company of the virtuous, abandoning his physical body, / he ascended to his own realm, which is difficult even for yogins to attain.
Then, when her son had departed, she felt grief in her heart; / yet on that very day, O king, she again took pleasure with paramours.
As she thus took pleasure together with paramours, O king, / in time old age arrived, which destroys charm and passion.
Abandoned by her lovers when seen with a body seized by old age, / she became a procuress, destroying good family and conduct.
Then she stole a cow along with its calf belonging to a brāhmaṇa; / and it was sold, O king, for a modest sum by her.
In this way some time was passed by her acting as a procuress, O king; / afterwards her body became withered and impaired.
When leprosy arose in her, five limbs fell away: / the two hands and the two feet, O king, and fifth, the nose.
When she, having become like this, could not obtain food from anywhere, / she was brought to the marketplace by a maidservant who lived there.
Lying there, that sinful woman, begging people with a pitiful / voice and uttering 'Fie!', filled her own belly.
Then nearby, a certain twice-born man, knower of the meaning of all scriptures / and a great orator, seeing her, spoke this word, O king:
'Sin brings sorrow to people in this world and the other; / therefore sin should not be committed by men who fear sorrow.
The person who, having committed a sin, indeed performs an expiation / does not practice it again and does not obtain its fruit.
He who repeatedly commits sins and performs no expiation, / his destiny is just like that of this sinful woman, in this world and the next.
By her a multitude of sins was accumulated in this world; / she reaps its fruit right here, and she will also suffer in hell.
In all the scriptures an expiation is seen for all sinful deeds; / but there is none for women who have completely turned away from proper conduct.'
Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, that best of twice-born bowed down to the sun and went away, / repeatedly remembering Viṣṇu, terrified at the sight of her.
Thus, fallen into misery and experiencing the fruit of the action / earned by herself, O king, she died in a few days.
No cremation rite was performed for that sinful woman; / she was dragged by the hair and carried outside the city by outcastes.
At the moment of her death, Yama's servants arrived; / causing her to assume a body of torment, they led her to the city of the son of the Sun.
To the righteous, that god is gracious in person, but to sinners he is hidden; / upon beholding her, he again turned his face away in aversion.
Turning his face away, Yama himself commanded his servants: / 'Let her be thrown at my word into the dreadful Raurava hell!'
Spoken to thus, his servants then took her and threw her into the dreadful Raurava [hell], / head downwards, remembering the deeds she had done.
Having remained there in Raurava for one manvantara, / she was afterwards born as an iguana in a cremation ground, eating the flesh of corpses.
There too for a hundred years she received the sorrow that was the fruit of her deeds, / making a ghastly diet of corpse flesh.
Once, that son of the sage who had been born from her womb, / wandering there in the cremation ground, arrived in a brāhmaṇa’s form.
Seeing her eating the flesh of corpses, the sage's son / meditated in his mind for a moment and recognized her as his own mother.
Having recognized his own mother, he said to himself: / The sage's son said: 'Today I will deliver her from this impassable ocean of sorrow!
Ah, no living creature is freed from the sinful karma it has committed / and amassed by itself, without reaching the end of the time of suffering!
Her time in hell, named after a Manu, has passed; / and now, through human reckoning, a hundred years have elapsed here.
How much of this terrible sin remains for her to endure?' / Nārada said: / Pondering thus, he closed his eyes and meditated once more with spiritual knowledge.
Having seen with divine vision the dreadful fate of that sinful woman, / that best of brāhmaṇas once more addressed himself, O king:
The sage's son said: 'Ah, no deliverance for her is seen even in a hundred kalpas, / without dying at a sacred tīrtha or taking refuge in the husband of Ramā;
or through the offering of piṇḍas performed by me at Gayā; / without this, she can have no good destination even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
And in this womb, these two could never happen for her: / death in the precincts of a tīrtha, or devotion to the worship of the husband of Śrī.
The cause of delivering her, who is sunk in an ocean of sin, / will indeed be the beneficial śrāddha performed by me at Gayā.'
Nārada said: / Having reflected thus, that righteous soul went to his father’s hermitage / and related to his father everything concerning the cause of his mother’s sorrow.
Hearing his son’s words announcing his mother’s misery, / that best of sages spoke to his son, whose neck was bent in reverence:
The sage said: 'O child, quickly rescue your mother from her misfortune, / as a prudent king rescues victory from an enemy in battle!
A son who does not deliver his mother and father / from suffering, if he is capable of delivering them, goes to hell.
Receiving water and piṇḍas from their own son at an excellent tīrtha, / ancestors go from hell to heaven, and from heaven to Hari's abode.
Therefore arise swiftly and go to the Khāṇḍava forest; / there is the holy Yamunā, frequented by the best of sages.
On its bank is Hariprastha, which contains all tīrthas; thence lies / holy Madhuvana, established there by Viṣṇu himself.
Having bathed there according to rule and performed your daily rites, / perform a śrāddha dedicated to her and carry out the rites for your mother.
When a śrāddha is performed by you there, desiring a good destination for her, / she will abandon her terrible iguana body and attain the world of Hari.
Whatever fruit is obtained, my child, by offering piṇḍas at Gayā, / a hundredfold greater than that is the merit declared by the virtuous at Madhuvana.
At present, my child, the sun is in the sign of Virgo; / go, my son, and perform the śrāddha for your former kinsfolk.'

6.214.m: Nārada said: / Hearing his father's words, he went with haste, / O king, to holy Madhuvana, which is a hundredfold greater than Gayā.
Inviting in the evening the brāhmaṇas who lived at that tīrtha, the knower of mantras, / having summoned them again at the proper time, spoke words of welcome.

Then, having washed their feet and worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, / he gave with pleasure water for the feet and arghya, and himself performed sipping of water with the proper side.

Then, having led those brāhmaṇas, he seated them in the place for the śrāddha, / having filled the ritual vessel along with kuśa grass, water, tulasī, flowers, perfume, unmutilated rice grains, and sesame,
and remembered the lotus-eyed Lord. / The twice-born recited three times the verse beginning with 'devatābhyaḥ'.
Then, with sesame and purified kuśa grass, he tied the ritual knot, / in order of the directions, beginning with the east, with the mantra 'agniṣvāttāḥ'.
With the mantra 'rakṣobhūta', he performed the tying of the waistband; / then, having made the solemn declaration, he gave seats of kuśa grass to the brāhmaṇas.
That best of brāhmaṇas then invoked the ancestors; / and having offered arghya into their hands, he inverted the vessel.

Having offered perfumes and other gifts, he again sipped water with the sacred thread on the left; / then the brāhmaṇa, shifting between the right and left positions of the thread, distributed the vessels.
Permitted by those brāhmaṇas, he then performed the offering into the fire; / O king, he filled those bowls with sacrificial oblations such as clarified butter.
Holding the vessels with palms turned neither upward nor downward, / instructed by the brāhmaṇas, he recited the verse 'pṛthvī te' for the twice-born.
With the mantra 'asaṃskṛtapraṇītānām', that brāhmaṇa / offered a seat of scattered food upon darbha blades whose tips pointed south.
With the mantra 'agnidagdha', he cast food mixed with ghee, / together with water, O king of kings, upon the seat prepared from kuśa grass.
Having again sipped water with the thread on the left, he gave a handful of water; / and asking, 'Are you satisfied?', they replied, 'We are satisfied.'
He received the permission of those twice-born to partake of the remaining food; / having made an altar one span in length for the piṇḍas, the brāhmaṇa
made a line pointing south with a darbha blade, O king, / and placed a burning ember in the south-east with the mantra 'ye rūpāṇi'.
Whoever was his mother and father in the previous birth, O lord of earth, / and who their parents were, and who were the paternal grandfathers, O king,

and who was the maternal great-grandfather, as well as the maternal grandparents, O best of kings— / directing the rite toward those six beginning with the father, together with their wives, according to rule,
having given seats of kuśa grass, he indeed offered six piṇḍas; / and having worshipped them with perfumes and the rest, he disposed of the middle piṇḍa.
Having done so and smelled it at his left shoulder, he placed down the piṇḍa vessel; / taking the water vessel at that time while reciting 'vāje vāje',
and having again offered water for washing feet and arghya, he satisfied them with dakṣiṇā and other gifts; / having accompanied them to the door and received their permission,
he himself, O king, that brāhmaṇa, ate together with his kinsmen. / Having thus completed the śrāddha, O best of kings, that best of twice-born,
for his former relatives at that holy Madhuvana, / when he, serene in soul, set out toward his father's hermitage—

Then, O king, all those recipients of the funeral offerings met him on the road, / mounted on six aerial chariots, adorned with divine ornaments, / clad in heavenly garments, and spoke to that best of Brahmins:
The ancestors said: / 'O dear child, tiger among Brahmins, choose an excellent boon! / By performing the śrāddha in this sacred place, you have redeemed us.
Through your grace, we have become attendants of the husband of Śrī. / Request, O wise one, whatever is desired in your heart.'
The son of the sage said: 'Who are you? From where have you come? Wherefore have you attained the status of attendants? / Why do you bestow a boon upon me without any service [done for you]?'
Nārada said: Having heard his words, the father from his previous birth— / who had died from sorrow after swallowing poison—spoke to his son:
The father said: / 'O Brahmin, I was your father in your previous birth, a Brahmin. / Deeply afflicted by my adulterous wife, your mother,
having fallen into extreme sorrow, I swallowed poison at night. / Having suffered an untimely death, I therefore became a night-roaming demon.
Thus, O dear child, a period of one hundred and fifteen / years passed while I was reduced to the state of a rākṣasa.
Now, however, when the śrāddha was performed by you in the sixteenth year here / at the sacred bathing place in the holy Madhuvana, I attained the state of a deity.
This aerial chariot comes from heaven, dispatched by Indra, / accompanied by attendants and a host of apsarases, in order to bear me away.
In order to grant you a boon here, together with attendants and the host of apsarases, / I ascended this excellent aerial chariot and, while going to heaven, have come [to you].
Choose a boon! May good betide you; we cannot delay. / Mounted on the elephant Airāvata, the lord of the gods awaits me.'
Nārada said: / Having thus told his story and bestowed upon his own son / the devotion to Hari requested by him, he went to heaven, O king.
Then his mother spoke to that son of her previous birth. / The mother said: 'Through your grace, I have become a goddess, released from sin.
Companionhood with Śacī has been attained by me, though I was sinful, O best of Brahmins, / once the śrāddha was performed by you here at the sacred place named Viśrānti.
Ask, O fortunate one, for the desire of your own heart; / I shall grant it to you, for the word of us goddesses is never false.
