You know that sin, O best of Brahmins, on account of which I became / a monitor lizard in a cemetery after residing for a long time in hell.
Give me leave, O son; the daughter of Puloman in heaven / awaits me in the sky, surrounded by troops of celestial women.'
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, that mother of his, free from selfish desire, / went to heaven, O king, after being saluted with his head by her own son.
Then his grandfather, bearing the likeness of Hari, / again spoke these words to that grandson, best of Brahmins:
The grandfather said: 'O dear child, dear child, live long! Receive what you desire! / Through your grace we have crossed the ocean of worldly existence, so hard to cross.
I am your grandfather, O child, and this is your grandmother. / Following me in death, that virtuous woman quickly attained residence in the same world.
Today, when the rite of the śrāddha was performed by you here at Viśrānti, / the world of Hari was attained by both of us, as well as his very form.'
Nārada said: Having spoken thus, together with that wife of his, O best of kings, / the Brahmin passed beyond the world of Brahmā and went to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, O ruler of kings, his great-grandfather spoke words, / which I shall relate to you today; listen with single-minded attention, O Brahmin:
The great-grandfather said: 'O child, O fortunate one, I am your great-grandfather. / As a consequence of killing a fetus, I entered the womb of a sow.
Having emerged from there, O dear child, afflicted by sin, I became a dog. / From that state, I became an immobile being on the Vindhya, the best of mountains.
There, having remained for a long time bearing the state of an immobile being, / I was violently uprooted by the roots by a certain elephant, O child.
Precisely at that time the śrāddha was performed by you / in this best of sacred places, O dear child; thus I was released from the immobile state.
Today an excellent residence has been attained [by me] in the city of the king of Yakṣas. / Grant your permission, best among Brahmins; through your grace I am going there.
Desiring to see you, I came here; you, of holy sight, have been seen by me, / as has Madhuvana, the best sacred place among all sacred places.'
Nārada said: Having been addressed thus by him, O lord of kings, that son of the sage, who knew dharma, / bowed with his head and inquired of his own great-grandfather:
The sage said: 'O dear father, you were born in the most venerable family of Brahmins; / how did you commit the sin named fetus-killing, O elder,
on account of which you entered into a succession of blameworthy wombs? / Explain, O highly fortunate one, if you still have memory of it.'
The great-grandfather said: 'Formerly, O tiger among Brahmins, in my birth as a Brahmin, / I made my livelihood by the application of mantras and yantras.
Out of greed for wealth, with my mind stricken by fate, / I gave medicine to women for the sake of their womb, and indeed for destroying [the fetus].
For greed robs people destitute of wealth of their wisdom, / just as the lord of the day [dries up] the water of streams in the summer season.
When wisdom is destroyed, O child, a person surely performs evil; / through evil he goes to hell, and then enters a vile womb.
At that time a certain pregnant woman asked me: / "O Brahmin, what shall I bring forth—a son or a daughter?"
Then I said to her: "You will have a daughter; / for the sake of the birth of a son, I shall give you a powerful medicine."
Addressed thus by me, that woman, the crest-jewel of foolish women, / grasped my feet and gave me a pala of gold.
And she said to me: “Six daughters have been born to me; / this seventh one has been predicted by you; she will not live upon birth.”
Act in such a way, O highly intelligent one, that I may not / give birth to another daughter, O Brahmin, which would destroy my own life."
Having heard her words, I spoke to her again: / “At the time of delivery, I shall provide medicine that produces a son.”
Saying, "So be it," she accepted my word and went home; / awaiting that time, she remained, trusting in my words.
When she was gone, O dear child, I became afflicted with anxiety / in this manner, O tiger among Brahmins; listen to that, I shall tell you:
"Trusting that a son would be born, she has given me a pala / of gold; I do not know what will become of her.
What should be done by me here? How could this gold, / weighing a pala, remain in the house of me, a poor man?"
Reflecting thus, a dreadful medicine that causes abortion / was caused by me to be given into her hands by her female servant, O dear child.
By means of that medicine, an abortion indeed took place for her then; / in the third month, the mark of male or female was not discernible.
Then, despondent on account of the miscarriage, she came to my house, / and, despairing of the birth of a son, asked for that gold back.
Then I showed her brick powder mixed with ash, / blended with turmeric powder, together with water:
"This powder was prepared by me, mother, for the birth of your son; / double the wealth of your gift was spent in accomplishing this."
Having spoken thus, O dear one, she left the powder and went home, / saying to me: “O best of the twice-born, I will take it from you in due time.”
"Thus, dear one, a very terrible murder of an embryo was committed by me, / through which I was made to wander in three vile wombs.
"By your grace I am now freed from the condition of an immovable being. / Grant permission, O best of sages! I shall go to auspicious Alakā."

Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, O king of kings, his great-grandfather, / bowed to with his head by him, departed toward the northern quarter,
on an extraordinary aerial chariot, garlanded with rows of jingling bells, / frequented by dancing Gandharvas, and adorned with jewel-studded enclosures.
Then, O great king, the great-grandmother of that brāhmaṇa, / mounted on an excellent aerial chariot, said to that great-grandson of hers:

The great-grandmother said:
"Nowhere else will you go by this merit, O you of good vows, / except to the abode marked by the lotus feet of the lord of Padmā.
"This husband of mine, your great-grandfather, was sinful, O sage; / though restrained by me, the wicked-minded one committed sin.
"Even he, very sinful in soul, has been saved by you from the ocean of suffering. / By whom indeed can a description of your virtues be made?"

Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, O king of kings, she too went to her husband's realm; / in Alakā she rejoiced together with that husband for a long time.
Then all those maternal grandfathers and others of that sage's son, / accompanied by their wives, mounted aerial chariots and went to heaven.
That best of the twice-born as well, having gone from that holy place to his father's hermitage, / narrated that whole story to his own father.
He too went there with his family to the forest of Madhu / and built a hut of leaves near Viśrānti.
Performing ablutions there at the Viśrānta holy place at the three times of day, / that best of sages felt no longing even for the realm of Viṣṇu.
Once, while bathing in the midst of the water, O king, that sage / yearned: "May a vision of Hari be mine at some time!"
As that best of sages was wishing thus, O king, / Hari, seated upon the king of birds, arrived in haste—
Hari, possessing four arms, together with Lakṣmī situated on his chest, / his body possessing the color of a fresh cloud, covered in garments colored like lightning,
with a noble chest radiant with the Kaustubha jewel, bearing a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, / his neck shining with a forest garland, wearing makara-shaped earrings,
having eyes like petals of a blooming lotus, his face adorned with fine locks of hair, / with nails shaped like coral, and red palms and soles of the feet.
He spoke to that best of the twice-born, illuminating [him] with the radiance of his teeth, / eclipsing the directions with an array [resembling] autumn moons.

The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the twice-born! This Madhuvana of mine is auspicious, / named Viśrānta, bestowing all desires through bathing [in it].
"Here, at the time of your bath, a vision of me was desired by you; / that which is difficult even for gods such as Brahmā to obtain has indeed been granted to you by me.
"Abandon this human body, O brāhmaṇa, and attain a divine one; / come to my abode with me, having mounted the lord of birds."

Nārada said:
Having heard this speech of that lord of Śrī, that chief among sages, / having bowed down right in the water, praised [him], O ruler of men.

The sage said:
"O lord of Śrī, whose lotus feet are caressed by the radiant lotus-[born goddess Lakṣmī], / I praise your [feet], which dispel the suffering of worldly existence, praised by the thirty [gods]!
"The creatures who are deluded here by your māyā, O Lord, / never have deliverance without your compassion.
"By serving true sacred places, O Lord, and likewise by the company of good people, / devotion arises among men through your grace.
"He who, having heard praise of your virtues spoken by many virtuous people, O Hari, / sings [it], which destroys all sins, does not fall into the cavity of a mother's womb.
"O lord of Śrī, the mind of your servant, though fallen into the great battle by chance / and covered with dust, does not lose its purity, just as an excellent jewel [does not].
"That man who falls like a staff at your lotus feet, bearing horripilation on his limbs, / leads his own family to your abode, which is desired by all yogis.

"Deluded by your māyā alone, O all-pervading Lord, the individual soul wanders on the paths of the universe; / through the charming corners of your eyes full of grace, he crosses the ocean of the universe in an instant."

Nārada said:
Having thus praised Govinda, that best of sages fell like a staff / at his feet, repeatedly crying: "Victory!"
The lord of Śrī, lifting up that best of sages who had fallen like a staff on the earth / with his arms, quickly placed him upon Suparṇa [Garuḍa].
And the Soul of the universe departed to Vaikuṇṭha with his family. / Thus has been related to you, O king, the auspicious [glory] of Madhuvana,
the glorification destroying all sins. What else do you wish to hear? / Uttering which or hearing which, a mortal is freed from all sins.

6.215.m:
Saubhari said:
Hearing these auspicious words of Nārada, O Yudhiṣṭhira, / King Śibi, son of Uśīnara, humbly said to him:

Śibi said:
"O sage, the glorification of Madhuvana has indeed been heard by me / from your mouth, but one doubt indeed remains in my mind:
"How was that virtuous soul, by whom all his relatives / from two births were delivered, the son of an unchaste woman?
"Explain this, O blessed one! You know everything in truth— / past, present, and future as well, O Nārada!"

Nārada said:
Once all the sages gathered at Haridvāra / on the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, endowed with all auspicious occasions.
Having bathed there according to the rules and performed their auspicious rites, / they sat peacefully on the ridge of the Himālaya.
There Budha, son of Tārā, arrived in the gathering of sages, / endowed with an abundance of beauty, like another embodied Smara.
Beholding him arrive, the chiefs among sages rose; / saluted by him with his head, they sat down again.
Beholding the honor given to Budha by the eminent sages, / that sage's son asked his own father, O Lord:

The sage's son said:
"Who is this that has arrived, dear father, another Smara in beauty, / to whom great honor has been shown by the best sages such as Vyāsa?"

Nārada said:
Hearing this utterance of his own son, that virtuous / tiger among sages spoke to the son who was filled with insistence:

The father said:
"Born from the belly of Tārā, the wise one named Budha is the son / of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, and the foremost founder of the lunar dynasty."

The son said:
"What disjointed speech has been spoken by you, father? / How can he who is the son of Bṛhaspati be the founder of the lunar dynasty?
"The Moon was born from the supreme sage Atri through Anasūyā, dear father. / How is this son of the preceptor of the gods the founder of his dynasty?
"This is a great doubt that exists in my mind, dear father. / Dispel it, O chief of the twice-born, for me, a child who is in doubt!"

The father said:
"Long ago, the glorious wife of Bṛhaspati, named Tārā, / was then abducted by force by the mighty Moon, dear son.
Having abducted her, he then brought the guru's wife to his own home in accordance with custom; / indeed, he took his delight with her for a long time.
From that, my dear child, in due course a pregnancy arose; / then Bṛhaspati requested his own wife [back].
Yet the Moon, overcome with arrogance and insolent from his strength, did not give [her up]; / then Bṛhaspati, my dear child, along with the gods headed by Śakra,
made preparations and set out to fight against the mighty Moon. / Śukra, with the Diti-born demons, in order to assist the Moon,
arrived then, my dear child, in that preparation for battle. / Thereupon, for Tārā's sake, a dreadful war broke out.
It is referred to by all people as the chief war known as the Tārakāmaya. / In that most terrible conflict, gods and demons were slain.
There was victory for no one, my dear child, nor was there defeat; / then Brahmā arrived and brought an end to that fierce combat.
Advising the lord of the night, he gave Tārā back to Bṛhaspati. / But Bṛhaspati, beholding Tārā pregnant then, / grew angry in the presence of Brahmā before the assembly of gods and Daityas.
Bṛhaspati said: / 'Listen to my word, Tārā of trembling gaze! / Whose is this child being carried in your womb? Does it belong to him or to me?'
The father said: / When questioned thus repeatedly, that modest, auspicious woman / did not say anything, my dear child, before him.
Then, while those gods and enemies of the gods were looking on, / he was born and, filled with anger, spoke these words to his mother:
Budha said: / 'Why, wicked woman, do you not name my father? / Abandoning modesty, behold the potency of my curse!'
The father said: / Having spoken thus, when he took up water and prepared to curse, / she softly said this: 'The Moon is your father.'
When it was thus spoken by that virtuous woman, the Moon, taking his own son / Budha, went joyfully to his own abode.
And Bṛhaspati, taking Tārā, went to his own house; / Brahmā, the gods, and the Daityas—they too went to their respective abodes.
All this has been related to you as you questioned me, / how this founder of the Lunar dynasty was born of Bṛhaspati's wife.
Nārada said: / Hearing this statement of his father, the sage's son laughed aloud, / and said to his own father: 'This one is a kuṇḍa, the son of an unfaithful woman!'
And the father said to his son: 'Alas, my son, do not utter this! / Knowing the inward heart of all creatures and aware of what you said, he will curse you.'
Nārada said: / When told this by that sage, the son of the Moon, knowing what was uttered, / spoke within hearing of all the sages, O king:
Budha said: / 'Let the tiger-like sages listen to my speech! / Whether it is sound or unsound, consider it without delay.
I came here in order to see you whose minds perceive reality; / I have not committed even the slightest offense against anyone.
Why do the arrogant despise me out of malice, / when I am longing for your sight in order to make my birth fruitful?
Indeed, such is the nature of the wicked: they agitate even innocent virtuous men / somewhere, just as sweet-voiced cuckoos [disturb the quiet].
The wicked do not relinquish their evil nature even in the company of the good, / just as the ocean does not shed its saltiness even through union with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Ah, the wickedness of the hunter! For he slays the forest-dwelling deer / who lead the life of sages in the forest, even though they understand his own song.
What wrong was done by fish to evil-hearted fishermen, / that they slay those swimming in sacred waters? For such is their nature.
The virtuous do not abandon their nature even when joined with the wicked, / just as sandalwood trees do not lose their coolness when surrounded by venomous, fiery serpents.
Do the virtuous dance upon the rise of another as if for their own side, / just as peacocks become delighted at a cloud, O best of sages?
For the virtuous yield even their own bodies for the sake of others, / just as my father's digits [are offered] for the sake of ancestors, gods, and men.
The rise of the virtuous is a cause of joy to the pure-hearted, / just as the rise of my father of cool rays is [a cause of joy] to the night-lotus flowers.'
Nārada said: / Having spoken these words, Budha in anger cursed that sage's boy: / 'You too shall quickly become a kuṇḍa on the surface of the earth!'
Hearing that curse uttered by Budha, the father / cast his own son at his feet, pleading, 'May he be forgiven!'
And he said: 'This boy does not understand your greatness; / it is not fitting for people like you to display anger toward this child.
The fundamental nature of a virtuous person who is angered for some reason remains forgiveness, / just as coolness remains the nature of water even when heated by fire.
Therefore, extending forgiveness quickly, bestow favor upon him, / a child devoid of discernment; for forgiveness is the essence of the virtuous.'
Nārada said: / Addressed thus by that sage, the son of the cool-rayed [Moon], / his mind calmed, abandoned anger and showed favor to him.
Budha said: / 'O sage, this boy of yours, having become a kuṇḍa on the surface of the earth / and having been given the sacred thread, shall indeed attain his own realm.'
Thus that sage's son, by the curse of Budha, O best of kings, / became a kuṇḍa on earth, by whom his ancestors were delivered.
A person who hears this sacred glorification of Madhuvana / obtains the complete fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Whatever men hold the excellent meaning of this glorification / in their heart, that [heart] is not overcome by sensual objects.
Those of great intellect who read or listen to this glorification / will, at the end of their bodies, reach the realm of Viṣṇu; there is no doubt.

This holy narrative of Madhuvana, which brings delight to the lord of Śrī, / has been described continuously to you by me—capable of destroying the mass of sins in the Kali age, and a cause of eliminating deviant paths when embodied in merit.
